acumen benchmark report

Overview

Per-run means over the valid split; error bars are standard errors.

Success across versions

Each line follows one model's success rate as the skill goes from no skill through each version. Solid lines are the valid tasks and dashed lines are the train tasks. The grey line is the mean across models and sits on top. The newest version has only valid runs, so the train lines stop one step short.

Cost vs. success

One mark per model and skill version, where colour is the model and the ✕ is that model's no-skill baseline. Arrows join one model's own marks in version order, baseline to v1 to v2 and on, so a chain is that model's path and never crosses to another. The grey mark pools every model for that version, with standard errors on both axes, and its chain is the pooled path. The staircase is the Pareto frontier: anything below and to the right of it is dominated, because something on the line costs less and succeeds more.

Is the difference real?

Each version is compared with the baseline on two separate questions: does it succeed more often, and does it cost less per run? Each is a one-sided test, and each is corrected on its own, with a Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery rate (FDR q) across the versions. Success is one family and cost is another, so a version can show a real gain on success, on cost, or on both, and the table says which. A gain the resampling cannot tell apart from noise leaves q high, which says the evidence is thin rather than that the version is bad. Best value in each column is bold, highest for the rates and lowest for cost and for the p- and q-values. On frontier is how often an arm holds the Pareto frontier across resamples. Resampling is over the 6 tasks, paired across arms, so the unit is the task rather than the run.

Did it help when it actually loaded?

If a skill never loads, the agent never reads it, so that run tells us nothing about the skill itself and only measures the baseline. Setting those runs aside lets us see whether the guidance helped in the runs where it did reach the agent. This helps tell apart a skill that fails to load from one that loads but still doesn't help. In the plot below, every dot is one model on one skill version. The colour shows the change in success rate against the baseline, green for better and red for worse. The size shows how often the skill loaded, and a hollow ring means it never did. Each loaded run is compared with the baseline on the very same task and model, and those differences are averaged, so the number is a real effect and does not depend on which tasks happened to load. It is still measured only on the tasks that loaded, and it does not test whether a gain is more than noise. For that, look at the significance test above.

Held-out test

This is the truly held-out split. It is benched once at the very end of a fit, on the best kept version and the baseline, and nothing in the loop ever sees it. Training learns from the train split and the best version is picked on valid, so the test split is the first and only place the skill meets these tasks. Read it as the honest final estimate of what the skill buys.

Skill version used for the held-out test: v2, the best on validation and the version to ship (acumen ship --skill v2).

Skill v2

parent: v1 · sha256:29e95380c590…

The wiki showed one dominant failure mode: the skill almost never loaded (0 of 3 in box,
composition, dotplot, and heatmap; 1 of 3 in volcano_r; 0 of 3 in volcano), with every hypothesis
tagged description-fixable. Reading the actual task prompts explained why: each task opens with
"You are completing one task in an automated benchmark. Your work is graded by a script, not read
by a human," yet v1's description sold the skill as an "Always-on persona ... write analysis code
a colleague can read" -- a pitch about human readability that is directly contradicted by the
task's own framing, so the agent reasonably judged it irrelevant. The description also read like a
toggleable command ("Always-on persona", with an on, off, status style argument-hint), which the
heatmap hypothesis flagged separately as looking like a manual switch rather than content to
auto-invoke. I rewrote the description to drop the persona and toggle framing and instead name the
category of goal actually present in every task -- writing or reviewing R or Python code that
computes a result or figure from experimental or omics data -- and to foreground what the body
actually prevents (silent bugs that change the final number: ad hoc recodes, positional joins,
unseeded randomness, AnnData view-vs-copy mistakes, double-filtering), which matches the
benchmark's real grading criterion, a correct answer.md, rather than human readability. I also
deleted a "Draft status, not assessed" line in the body, which could only ever undercut the
skill's authority on the rare run where it did load. Finally, for volcano (noskill tagged
body-fixable: runs disagree on the exact significant-gene count because each invents its own
low-count pre-filter before the DESeq2 fit, which changes the multiple-testing universe and shifts
the count), I added one generic rule to the existing checks "do not write" list against layering an
invented filter or cutoff in front of a method that already filters or corrects internally --
applicable to any statistical method, not tied to this dataset or package, so it should generalise
rather than overfit. I left the heatmap and volcano_r regressions alone beyond the description fix:
drilling into the one run where volcano_r's skill did load showed the agent correctly deprioritized
the skill's project-layout conventions, per the existing order-of-authority rule, and the run's
failure was a sandbox write-hook falsely rejecting the script path -- unrelated to skill content and
explicitly tagged not-skill-fixable, so no body change addresses it.

Skill v3

parent: v2 · sha256:41dd300d7b9c…

Checked REGRESSIONS.md first: the heatmap and volcano_r drops at v1 were caused by an unrelated sandbox Write-hook stall (max_turns, no answer.md) in runs where the skill hadn't even loaded, not by anything v1 added to the skill body — both recovered to their noskill pass rate by v2, so there was nothing in the current (v2-derived) body to reverse.

Across box/composition/dotplot/heatmap/volcano_r the wiki consistently shows the skill loading inconsistently (0/3-2/3) but never changing the outcome, since the model already solves these standard scanpy/pandas patterns correctly unaided — per the instructions, a load-rate gap with no outcome effect is lower-value than a body gap that changes outcomes, so I left the description untouched rather than risk overfitting it further.

The one task with a real, outcome-changing, body-fixable gap is volcano: across noskill/v1/v2 the pseudobulk+PyDESeq2 pipeline is fully specified by the task prompt (exact threshold, design, contrast, alpha), yet agents still land on slightly different significant-gene counts (835/838/839) because each hand-rolls the pseudobulk aggregation and the covariate dtypes differently, with no check to catch a silent row-count/total mismatch or an accidentally-numeric grouping covariate. I added two generalizable fixes to the body (not tied to this dataset): (1) a new default check that a grouped aggregation (pseudobulk, groupby-sum) must produce exactly one row per group and conserve each column's total, since two equivalent-looking implementations (groupby vs. one-hot-matmul) can silently drop/duplicate rows; (2) sharpened the existing "set factor levels explicitly" rule to call out that a blocking/grouping covariate (batch, replicate, donor) in a model formula must be cast to character/factor, since a numeric ID silently fits as a continuous slope instead of one coefficient per level with no error. Both match the skill's existing "silent data loss" check philosophy and should reduce run-to-run variance on any aggregate-then-model pipeline, not just this one.
